sentences.text: The upper jaw of this dinosaur includes a bone with a front opening and other bones riddled with holes of different shapes and sizes.
Its snout is straight and hollow, formed by an elongated upper bone that creates a U-shape when viewed from below.
The lower jaw bones also show signs of modification, featuring a basic grinding surface on the inner top.
The front part of the lower jaw bone is bent at a sharp angle of 32 degrees.
Large oval holes run along the length of the lower jaw platform, which might be leftover spots where teeth once sat.
A strong upward projection on the side bone of the jaw suggests powerful biting muscles.
The single known skeleton belongs to a young dinosaur rather than an adult.
Evidence of past attacks is preserved on the skull, showing two visible marks from another creature's teeth.
The species name translates to 'the diminutive,' highlighting the small size of this particular fossil.
A skeleton was found in 2008 by an international team exploring the Altan Uul III site in the Gobi Desert.
Scientists named and described the species Gobiraptor minutus in 2019.
This specific skeleton dates back to the early Maastrichtian, roughly seventy million years ago.
The remains include parts of the skull, lower jaws, pelvis, thigh bones, and the left foot.
Only one incomplete specimen, cataloged as MPC-D 102/111, is known to science.
Its thick lower jaws were likely built for crushing hard items like bivalves, seeds, and tough plants.
Experts believe it was not a meat-eater because its foot structure did not support fast running.
The claws on its feet were only slightly curved.
The tail base vertebra has large air-filled spaces on its sides and a long groove underneath.
The ribs attached to the sacrum were very sturdy and longer than the spine segment they joined.
Projections at the front of the tail joint likely restricted how much the tail base could move.
The shoulder blade was not fused to the socket, a trait that indicates the animal was young.
Studies suggest this dinosaur was not closely related to other similar birds living in the same area.
It is placed in the family Oviraptoridae within the suborder Oviraptorosauria.
This animal lived at the end of the Cretaceous period in what is now Asia.
The fossil comes from the Nemegt Formation, which dates to the early Maastrichtian stage.
The Maastrichtian stage spans from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
It inhabited a wet environment that was also partially dry.
The habitat is described as a moderately dry middle zone.
Some researchers suspect this might actually be a young member of a different family, the Caenagnathidae, misidentified because its thickened jaw front is a trait seen in that group.
